title: 3-Read Friday #47: Testing, Implementation, and Simple Versus Easy
author: Craig Barton
summary: This issue's three picks are unified by a shared diagnostic habit: figure out what's really going on before reaching for a fix. Barton opens with Claudia Lewis's response to a poorly-gone test, which begins by asking whether the result was actually a surprise before recommending next steps. He follows with Peter Foster's post on leading change, aimed at anyone from Head to classroom teacher, which Barton notes uses the same diagnose-before-you-solve structure as Lewis's piece. He closes with Blake Harvard's distinction between a 'simple' classroom and an 'easy' one, which Barton frames as a useful reminder that routines, predictability and safety are what let students perform at their best, independent of how demanding the actual content is.
points: Barton explicitly notes the structural parallel between Lewis's and Foster's posts: both insist on diagnosing the nature of a problem before jumping to a solution.
He frames test-result response as contingent on whether the outcome was a surprise, changing the recommended next steps depending on the answer.
He highlights Harvard's simple-versus-easy distinction as valuable specifically for its emphasis on routines, predictability and safety as performance enablers.
The issue as a whole models a diagnostic mindset applicable at classroom, department, and whole-school levels of change.
quotes: You gave your students an end-of-topic test... and it has not gone well.
Claudia asks us first to consider whether this result was a surprise.
And depending on our answer, she has some super practical next steps to take.
Pete, like Claudia above, asks us first to consider the nature of the issue, which then leads to the solution.
This is a really useful distinction from Blake, focussing on the importance of routines, predictability and safety to ensure students can perform to their very best.
